Joseph-Louis Lagrange. The Italian-born mathematician and astronomer who became one of the most influential figures of the eighteenth century.

Born in Turin in seventeen thirty-six, Lagrange worked at the Berlin Academy under Frederick the Great for twenty years before moving to Paris, where he flourished during the revolutionary turmoil. He revolutionized calculus through the calculus of variations, developed a new approach to mechanics using abstract mathematical principles, and advanced algebra, number theory, and numerical analysis.

His elegant methods remain fundamental tools across mathematics and physics. He developed the calculus of variations, generalizing calculus to optimize entire functions rather than isolated variables. This unified approach became fundamental to mathematical physics. He introduced Lagrange multipliers to solve constrained optimization problems, finding extrema of a function subject to equality constraints by introducing auxiliary variables. He reformulated classical mechanics using the principle of least action, where a physical system evolves to extremize the action integral. This was equivalent to Newton's laws but more elegant and generalizable.

Lagrange formulated the Lagrangian function as kinetic minus potential energy, leading to the Euler-Lagrange equations that govern motion. These differential equations replace Newton's F equals ma in his formalism. He made deep contributions to number theory, including the theory of quadratic forms, continued fractions, and representation by sums of squares. He also advanced the theory of polynomial equations and their resolvents.

The Lagrange interpolation formula constructs a unique polynomial passing through given data points and remains indispensable in numerical analysis. He developed fundamental results in calculus, including the mean value theorem, and in the theory of differential equations. His contributions unified mechanics, calculus, and number theory, establishing him as arguably the greatest mathematician of the eighteenth century.
